$comment: Model rates in USD per million tokens. DATA, not code -- and that is this file's
whole argument. One price table in this repository lived with the vendor
(the vendored claude-history server, _PRICING) and went stale on April
2026: every new model fell through to Sonnet's default rate, so an Opus 5 session
read three times cheaper than it was. A price table goes stale -- so let it go stale
in a data file that has a date rather than in code that does not.
THE KEY IS MODEL x SPEED. `message.usage.speed` really does stand in a session's
record (measured on CR-2608-f9b6: `standard` on 5 367 turns, `fast` on 0, the field
absent on 2 996 -- sessions from Claude Code 2.1.234). Fast mode is therefore a
measurable item rather than a hypothesis, and gets its own `<model>:fast` entry.
THE FAST RATES ARE WRITTEN DOWN, NOT COMPUTED. Fast mode is $10 input and $50
output per MTok, available for Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 alone. The cache multipliers stack
ON THE FAST PRICE, so a 5 min write = 1.25 x 10 = 12.50, an hourly write = 2 x 10 =
20, and a hit = 0.1 x 10 = 1.00. Those three numbers stand here as numbers: this file
is a price list rather than a calculator, and a reader is not to recreate the
multipliers from memory.
FABLE 5.1 READS ITS CACHE AT 0.025 x, NOT 0.1 x. $0.25 per MTok against a $10 input
is a quarter of Fable 5's $1.00 and looks like a misplaced decimal; it is the rate.
Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 are the only models with that multiplier -- every
other entry here is the standard 0.1 x -- so the two lines below are the reason a reader
must not derive a cache rate from the input rate, on this table or any other.
A MISSING `:fast` ENTRY IS INFORMATION, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. Opus 4.7 errors on
`speed: "fast"`, and Opus 4.6 runs standard and is priced that way. That is why
`pricing.rate()` must not fall through to the standard rate when somebody asks about
`claude-opus-4-7:fast` -- a missing rate is an answer.
What is NOT here and why: the 1.1 x multiplier for `inference_geo: "us"`, because a
session's record carries no geography at all, and a rate applied on a guess lies
exactly as much as a stale one. `batch_discount` is here, but it applies only where
`service_tier` in the record says `batch`.
Updating: raise `as_of`, correct the numbers, leave the entries of retired models --
the session corpus is older than the current line-up and has a right to be priced.
The aliases a dispatch is sometimes named with instead of a resolved identifier.
Measured: one of CR-2608-f9b6's 82 dispatches has `model: "sonnet"`, because the
parent did not record a `resolvedModel`. The subagent's file knows the truth and the
parser takes it from there, but an alias has to resolve when that file is absent too.
AN ALIAS NAMES THE RELEASE A BARE TIER NAME MEANS NOW, not the one it meant when the
entry was written. A record reaches this map only because the client did not resolve
the id, so the alias is a statement about what is being dispatched today -- and today
a bare `fable` is Fable 5.1. Repointing it re-prices nothing that exists: measured
over `retro/` and `spec/changes/`, no archived record carries a bare `fable`, `opus`,
`sonnet` or `haiku` at all, and every resolved fable id in the local session corpus
is `claude-fable-5-1`. The retired entries stay in the table above for the records
that DO name a release; that is what they are for.
A fixed set of scenarios: the same tokens, one rate. `model: null` means
"price each model at its own rate", that is the actual state. The rest move EVERY
bucket -- the parent's and the subagents' -- onto one rate, in order to answer the
question "and what if all of this ran on one model".
